name: PT Lotte Chemical Titan Tbk

frontmatter.title: Lotte Chemical Titan: the inventory turned into cash, the spread did not turn into margin
frontmatter.summary: FPNI runs one polyethylene plant, buys its ethylene inside the Lotte group and earns a thin spread. The third quarter sold the inventory the first half built; we now credit the September net cash, which ties to the half-year statements, though about three-fifths of the quarter's operating cash flow is still unexplained. We hold at HOLD with a target of Rp378, 1.0% total return.
thesis: One plant, one product, one internal supplier: the Merak plant has 450 kt of capacity and sold 312.7 kt in FY2025, buying essentially all its feedstock from a Lotte group company — trade payables to related parties were US$55.6m against US$29.0m of cash [S3, S4].

The third quarter resolved the inventory question against the margin and in favour of the cash flow: the spread fell back from the second-quarter spike even as revenue set a record, the finished-goods build was sold, and cash rose to nearly half the market value of the company [S0, S4].

The market is paying for more than we can evidence: the reverse DCF implies 6.9% FY2027E revenue growth against our 4.0%, and the base value of Rp381 is barely above the Rp374 price, far below the cost of equity, even with the September net cash credited [S0, S4].

The base case is deliberately unheroic — a mid-cycle gross margin of 3.9% held to perpetuity, below the second-quarter 2026 print and above the four-year trough average, with no trade remedy and no disposal in it [S3, S4].

Optionality is real and unpriced: the parent has revived a disposal process for its Indonesian unit, and the industry is lobbying for anti-dumping and safeguard duties that would lift utilisation from 60-70% toward the level the association asks for [S5, S8].

catalysts.event: Government response to the Inaplas trade-remedy request on dumped polyethylene imports

blocks.text: This results note follows the HOLD we published on 6 November and keeps it. We hold PT Lotte Chemical Titan at HOLD with a twelve-month target of Rp378, 1.0% against the Rp374 price and 1.0% total return — below the 11.0% cost of equity, which is what the rating tests; no dividend is modelled, because none has been paid [S0]. The target rises from the published level because the third-quarter cash is now credited: the pack's cash series ties to the archived half-year statements at both dates, so the item that stripped the September uplift is removed, and the full-year revenue build is corrected to the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate. The target is the probability-weighted average of three scenario values — Rp130 in the bear, Rp381 on our most likely path and Rp804 if trade remedies land — and the parent's disposal is unvalued in all three.

The reason for the change is not a better spread. The third quarter printed a gross margin of roughly four and a half per cent, which is the level the base case had already assumed for the long run, and it was half the second-quarter print [S0]. What the quarter delivered is real but not investable at this price on our evidence. It sold the finished-goods build the first half had accumulated, so inventories came back down and operating cash flow turned strongly positive, and the pack shows cash of about half the market value with negligible debt at 30 September [S0]. That balance now ties to the filings at the top: the pack's cash line equals cash plus short-term investment in the half-year statements at both the December and June dates, and the third-quarter build is corroborated by the inventory release from the June figure the interim notes carry [S0, S4, F21, F27, F22]. What does not reconcile is the composition of the quarter's operating cash flow: about three-fifths of it is not explained by the pack's own EBITDA, inventory, receivables and payables lines [S0]. We credit the September net cash in full and carry the cash-flow composition gap as a risk the FY2026 audit will test, not as a deduction from value. Revenue also ran above the H1 pace and nine months are within a tenth of the whole of FY2025's revenue [S0], but the base case is worth Rp381, barely above the Rp374 price and below the cost of equity, and the market is discounting FY2027E revenue growth of 6.9% against our 4.0%: the shares are priced for more growth than we can evidence. What we are not paying for is a trade remedy or the parent's disposal; both remain outside the base case, which is why the target sits above the base value rather than at it.

The margin is the whole thesis, and the sensitivity is not small: one point of perpetual gross margin moves the twelve-month value by about six per cent in either direction, two points takes more than a third off on a narrowing while the mirror widening adds about an eighth, and the bear's two points take the value to Rp130 - the September net cash less about a year of the modelled burn, not zero. That is why the bear is a margin case and why the third-quarter print matters more than the revenue record.

The dispersion is still the point: this is a thin-margin commodity converter whose equity is an option on the polyethylene-ethylene spread, and a reader who puts no weight on a trade remedy should work from the base value of Rp381 — which, with the September cash credited, is barely above the price and below the cost of equity.

The company is the listed remnant of the old Titan petrochemical group. It owns, through a subsidiary it controls almost entirely, a single polyethylene plant at Merak in Banten that makes HDPE and LLDPE, and a small import-and-trading book that buys Malaysian PE and PP for resale [S3, S4]. It does not own the new Cilegon cracker that the President inaugurated in 2025 and in which Danantara was offered a minority; that asset sits outside the listed entity, and the market's 2025 re-rating of the shares appears to have conflated the two [S6, S3]. The cracker is nevertheless the reason the payable exists: of the US$55.6m owed to related parties at end-2025, US$53.0m is owed to PT Lotte Chemical Indonesia, up from nil a year earlier, so the new domestic cracker is already the feedstock source [S3]. A same-site ethylene supplier removes the import freight, the duty and the three-to-six-week lead time of a merchant cargo, and it is the structural reason the plant can run at all; we do not put a number on that advantage because no archived source prices it, so it stays as upside narrative rather than a bull-cash-flow item [S3]. The same relationship carries contracted income the other way: the group's trading arm acts as agent in Indonesia and earns a marketing commission from its affiliates, and it leases the ethylene tank and auxiliary facilities to the Indonesian cracker on a long finance lease, whose cash receipt was US$0.4m in the first half [S4, F34] — a fraction of a per cent of revenue, so it is immaterial to the model, while the lease receivable sits inside other receivables and is therefore already in the book value. What is left is a converter: it buys ethylene, polymerises it, and keeps the difference.

That difference was negative for most of the last three years. Gross profit was US$-4.0m in FY2024 and US$1.4m in FY2025, against revenue of US$368.0m and US$320.7m [S3]. The FY2025 net profit of US$4.3m is not evidence of a recovery: it came from other gains of US$11.3m and a tax benefit, while the operating line lost US$-8.3m [S3]. What did change is 2026, when reported gross profit reached US$14.2m in the first half and revenue grew by double digits [S4]. But the half is not clean evidence of a wider spread. Unit feedstock cost was roughly unchanged — raw materials used rose to US$160.2m on 163.3 kt of feedstock in the half, and the cost per tonne barely moved — while the plant ran far harder and the half built US$29.4m of finished goods it did not sell [S4, F19, F31, F32]. Charge production rather than sales to the period and the half is a small loss. The third quarter then answered the question the half left open, and the answer was not the one the bulls wanted: the spread fell back to roughly the level the base case carries, and it was the sale of the inventory, not the spread, that produced the quarter's cash [S0]. That distinction is the whole of our caution on the near-term earnings, and it is now confirmed rather than suspected.

Three things move the value. The first is the spread, which is set by Asian olefin supply and by how much polymer China and the Middle East push into Indonesia; national utilisation is only 60-70% because of dumped imports, and the industry association is asking for anti-dumping and safeguard duties [S8]. The second is the group relationship: with almost all feedstock bought from a related party, the transfer price inside Lotte is the single largest determinant of the minority's margin, and the company's own filings warn that related-party terms may differ from arm's length [S3, S4]. The third is the parent's exit. Lotte Chemical Corp has revived a process to sell its Indonesian unit, which is the event that could hand the minority a control price; no decision has been announced [S5].

Polyethylene is one of the most widely traded commodity polymers, and its price in Asia is quoted
against the ethylene contract price rather than against a domestic index. Producers without their
own cracker are pure converters: their margin is the polymer-to-monomer spread less conversion cost,
and they carry no upstream integration benefit when the monomer is short. A converter's competitive
position therefore depends on logistics, customer service and the credit it extends to distributors
rather than on resource ownership.

PT Lotte Chemical Titan Tbk (formerly PT Titan Kimia Nusantara) was listed in 2002 and took its present name in 2013 [S3]. It operates in two pieces. The operating subsidiary, PT Lotte Chemical Titan Nusantara, is 450 kt of installed polyethylene capacity at Merak, Cilegon, built on an INEOS Innovene fluidised-bed process and producing high-density and linear low-density polyethylene for film, injection, blow moulding and cable applications [S3]. The parent company above it runs an import and distribution book of PE, PP and BOPP film, largely bought from the Malaysian affiliate, and earns a commission on marketing services [S3]. Own-product PE is the whole business: it generated US$318.1m of FY2025 revenue, while trading revenue was small enough to be immaterial [S3].

Volume has run below capacity. Sales were 312.7 kt in FY2025 against 450 kt of nameplate, split between domestic and export, and production fell because of maintenance and feedstock availability [S3]. Domestic sales volume declined while export volume rose, and both domestic and export selling prices fell year on year [S3, F24, F25]. Management describes its response as selective and measured adjustment of plant utilisation rather than a shutdown [S3]. The product is sold largely into the domestic market to converters and distributors, and one customer, PT Bukitmega Masabadi, took 35.8% of net revenue in H1 2026 [S4] — a concentration that matters for pricing and for receivables.

The company is controlled by Lotte Chemical Titan International Sdn. Bhd., which holds 92.5% of the shares; the free float is 7.5% [S3, S0]. The chain runs up through Lotte Chemical Titan Holding Berhad in Malaysia to Lotte Chemical Corporation in Korea, and the ultimate shareholder is the Shin Dong Bin family vehicle [S3]. There are 304 employees [S0]. The group structure matters more than usual here: the same chain that controls the company also supplies its feedstock, so the minority's economics are set inside a relationship it does not control [S3].

The strategy that follows from this is defensive rather than expansionary. The company does not integrate backwards into a cracker, it does not add a second product family, and it spends below its depreciation charge; management's stated lever is the utilisation rate, flexed between the domestic and export books depending on which market pays the better net price [S3, F24, F25]. The domestic book is the larger and the more profitable one, and the export book has been the swing channel when import pressure closes the home market [S3]. Against Indonesian converters the company is one of a small number of local polyethylene producers and therefore a challenger to imported resin rather than to a domestic peer, which is a better position than the utilisation numbers suggest and a worse one than the brand of an integrated producer would give it [S8]. The customer base is narrow and industrial — converters who turn resin into film, bags and moulded parts — so the company's revenue tracks packaging demand and the credit cycle in the domestic economy rather than any consumer brand of its own [S3, S4].

Indonesian petrochemical demand grows with the packaging and consumer cycle, but the domestic industry is not capturing that growth. The olefin and plastics association puts national plant utilisation at 60-70% and describes domestic producers as under severe pressure from imports priced at dumping levels, with several facilities having stopped operating altogether [S8, S9]. The association wants safeguard and anti-dumping instruments applied so that utilisation can return to the level it says the industry needs, and the Ministry of Industry has said it will inventory the obstacles and use available instruments including the national standard and anti-dumping policy [S8]. A separate request asks for the zero import duty on LPG feedstock to be made permanent [S8].

The structural problem is capacity, not demand. Chinese and Middle Eastern polymer capacity built through the last cycle is exported into a region that already has surplus, and Indonesian producers without a captive cracker sit at the high end of the cost curve: they pay a merchant ethylene price and compete with integrated producers on the same product. That is the cost-curve position, and it is weak. The company's defence is not cost but proximity — a domestic plant with short lead times and rupiah-denominated service into a market where imported resin carries freight, duty risk and credit terms — plus a parent that can extend feedstock credit, which the balance sheet shows it does through related-party payables [S3].

On the five forces: supplier power is high and concentrated, because the feedstock is bought inside the group and the group sets the terms [S3, S4]; buyer power is high, with a single distributor at 35.8% of revenue and commodity-grade product that can be sourced from imports [S4, S8]; the threat of substitutes is low for PE in its applications but the threat of import competition is severe and is the binding constraint today [S8]; rivalry is high, with national utilisation far below full and price the only differentiator; and barriers to entry are high for a new plant but irrelevant, because the competition arrives as imported resin rather than as a new Indonesian plant. The moat is therefore thin. The one genuine asset is the installed plant, and the company itself prices it. The property, plant and equipment note in the half-year statements carries an independent valuation of property, plant and equipment at US$145.9m as at 31 December 2024, prepared by KJPP Stefanus Tonny Hardi on Level-three inputs, using the market data approach for land and the cost approach for the other assets, and management states that the valuation remains relevant to 30 June 2026 [S4, F35]. That is about two and a half times the plant’s carrying amount of US$56.9m [S4, F36] and nearly three times the enterprise value our discounted cash flow produces (US$54.1m). The divergence is real and we do not explain it away: a cost-approach appraisal of a single-train plant is a rebuild-cost figure, struck on Level-three inputs with no transaction behind it, while the cash flow values the same assets at what they earn, and at a mid-single-digit spread they earn almost nothing. The gap is precisely why the plant has strategic value to an operator that brings its own ethylene, so we carry it as the reason a trade buyer could pay more than the market does, not as a value in the model. The parent’s disposal process [S5] is the only route by which a buyer could pay for it, and with no stake, price or buyer disclosed it stays unvalued optionality in the base and the bull.

Regulation cuts both ways. Trade remedies would be the single largest positive for the domestic spread [S8]; the free-float question is the largest structural negative, because a 7.5% public holding against a controlling shareholder at 92.5% [S3] leaves the minority with no pricing power over any corporate action, and the regulator's fifteen per cent free-float minimum, phased in over three years from the March 2026 rule, dates the problem rather than leaving it in the background [S26, S3]. The macro deck's rupiah path matters only indirectly, since the company reports in US dollars and sells partly in the domestic market where import parity sets the price; Brent matters through the naphtha-linked ethylene contract, which is why the model carries a small crude link rather than a large one [S0].

Revenue fell from US$473.9m in FY2022 to US$320.7m in FY2025 as both price and volume declined, and the cost base did not follow: cost of goods sold was US$319.3m against revenue of US$320.7m, leaving a gross profit of US$1.4m [S3]. The operating loss was US$-8.3m once US$9.7m of selling and administrative expense was charged [S3]. The reported net profit of US$4.3m therefore flatters the business twice over: other gains of US$11.3m and a net tax benefit carried the year, and the tax benefit itself reflects a group that has been loss-making long enough to accumulate a deferred tax asset [S3].

The first half of 2026 is the first period in three years in which the reported gross margin reached a normal converter's level. Revenue was US$176.9m and gross profit US$14.2m [S4] — a reported margin well above the 6.0% we carry for the full year. Raw materials were US$160.2m — the ethylene line is effectively the entire cost of goods sold [S4]. The half is not, however, a clean read of the spread, and this is the single most important adjustment in the model. The cost-of-goods note shows cost of goods manufactured of US$180.4m plus finished-goods purchases, against revenue of US$176.9m: charging what the plant produced rather than what it sold, the half lost money, because finished goods rose to US$29.4m from a much smaller opening balance after a drawdown in the first half of 2025 [S4, F30, F31]. The reported gross profit is therefore partly a deferral, not a gain, and it is recoverable only if the inventory is sold at the spread the half earned. The third quarter shows what happened when it was sold: revenue rose again and gross profit fell, because the inventory carried a cost basis built at the second quarter's prices and the spread on new production was thinner [S0]. The deferral was released into cash, not into margin.

Actual against forecast is now a nine-month question, and the answer is that the year has run ahead of the revenue line and behind the margin line. On nine months to September 2026 revenue was well above the same period a year earlier — within a tenth of the whole of FY2025's revenue — with the third quarter the strongest of the year [S0]; the gross margin on the other hand came in below the second-quarter spike and close to what we carry in perpetuity [S0]. Our FY2026E revenue of US$397.8m is therefore the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at about the third-quarter level, and the FY2026E gross margin of 6.0% is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter exit rate, not an annualisation of the second quarter [S0]. The one line we cannot verify against a filing is the quarterly detail itself: the company's investor site still carries only the mid-year 2026 statements [S10], no nine-month statement has been archived and no press story reports the quarter, so the third-quarter figures in this note come from the data pack alone [S0]. That is a sourcing gap, stated rather than hidden, and it is the first thing the FY2026 audit will test.

The cash is the part of the quarter that matters, and the balance now ties to the filings even where its composition does not. Inventories fell back from the June peak, operating cash flow turned strongly positive after the first half's outflow, and the pack shows cash about two-thirds higher than the June balance against negligible debt at 30 September [S0]. The balance is corroborated twice over: the pack's cash line equals cash plus short-term investment in the half-year statements at both dates, and the inventory release starts from the June figure the interim notes carry [S4, F21, F27, F22]. What does not reconcile is the composition of the quarter's operating cash flow — about three-fifths of it is not explained by the pack's own EBITDA, inventory, receivables and payables lines [S0]. We therefore credit the September balance and treat the cash-flow gap as a risk the audit will test, not as a deduction from value. Two further caveats belong beside it. Receivables rose faster than revenue in the quarter, to a level well above the June ratio, so not all of the quarter's revenue had been collected by the period end [S0]; and the cash sits alongside a related-party payable of similar size, so the liquidity is the group's supplier credit as much as it is the company's own earnings [S3, F15, F28]. Both are optics-class rather than manipulation-class — the balances are disclosed and the counterparty is the feedstock supplier — but they are why we treat the net cash as a buffer to be valued, not as surplus to be distributed.

Our forecast reproduces the last actual and then normalises. FY2026E revenue of US$397.8m is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate [S0]; FY2027E adds 4.0%, which is demand growth rather than a capacity-fill rate because the plant is already running at a level the sector's import pressure caps [S8]; and from FY2028E revenue grows at roughly Indonesian PE demand [S8]. The gross margin is the swing factor: 6.0% in FY2026E, the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter exit rate; 4.2% in FY2027E, which the crude link delivers at about the third-quarter spread as the second-quarter spike is competed away; and 3.9% in perpetuity — above the four-year trough average and below the second-quarter print [S3, S4, S0]. We restate depreciation from the financial statements, not the data pack: the real charge was US$7.3m in FY2025 and US$6.5m in FY2024, several times the pack's figure, which turns the reported EBITDA of a near-zero number into a small negative one [S3, F5, F6].

Cash conversion was the flag, and the third quarter reversed it. H1 2026 operating cash flow was US$-7.2m despite the reported gross profit, because inventories rose to US$48.1m and finished goods to US$29.4m from a much smaller opening balance [S4, F22, F31]. Some of that was a deliberate restock ahead of price; some was production running ahead of sales, which in a falling-price market is the classic way a converter destroys value. The accruals ratio is not meaningful in a year with a tax benefit, but the divergence was: gross margin expanded while operating cash went negative, and the expansion was the inventory. We treated this as an optics-class flag rather than a manipulation-class one — the build is disclosed line by line and carried at the lower of cost and net realisable value [S4] — and the third quarter has now closed it: the inventory was sold, the cash came back, and the margin with it [S0]. The lesson for the forecast is that this company's cash flow follows inventory turns, not the spread, which is why we model the working-capital cycle explicitly rather than letting it fall out of revenue. Capex is maintenance only at US$2.9m in FY2025 [S3], below depreciation, so the asset base is shrinking in real terms — a plant being harvested rather than grown. We do not carry that harvest into perpetuity: the DCF runs capex at the maintenance rate through FY2031E and then at the D&A rate from FY2032E, because a terminal growing at 2.0% has to reinvest at least its depreciation to exist. The near-term cash release is real; the perpetual one is not.

The balance sheet is the strong part, and it is now documented through September. At 30 June 2026 the company held US$29.0m of cash and a further US$6.2m of short-term investment against negligible debt [S4]; the pack's 30 September figure is about two-thirds higher, corroborated by the inventory release and by the exact tie of the pack's cash line to the half-year statements [S0, S4, F22]. Book equity is now close to the market value of the company. The working capital is unusual: trade payables to related parties were US$55.6m against a token third-party balance, which means the parent effectively finances the feedstock [S3]. That is a real source of liquidity and a real governance exposure at the same time — the September cash is the mirror of the September payable, and the two move together. Capital allocation has been conservative to the point of inertia: no dividend in any year the data pack covers, capex below depreciation, and cash accumulating [S0, S3]. Our base case assumes no payout; any distribution would be additive to the return. The dividend capacity is real even though the payout is not modelled: at the base case's through-cycle free cash flow, and with the net cash on the balance sheet, a distribution would be covered several times over; the constraint is governance, not cash. A parent at 92.5% that has never taken a dividend is the reason we do not credit it, and we model permanent retention because that is the observed behaviour, treating any distribution as upside.

We value FPNI on a discounted cash flow, at a cost of equity of 11.0% and a WACC of 11.0%, built from a risk-free rate of 5.0%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5% and the industry's unlevered beta of 0.90, taken from the house cost-of-capital inputs and the macro deck rather than from the data pack. The company is effectively unlevered, so the WACC is the cost of equity. A commodity converter with a merchant feedstock and a single plant deserves no premium to that discount rate, and the terminal growth of 2.0% is deliberately below Indonesian nominal growth because the asset has no moat to protect a perpetual growth premium [S5].

The DCF gives an enterprise value of US$54.1m, of which 25.0% is terminal value, and an equity value of Rp344 a share [S0]. The terminal value is a minority of the total, not the whole of it: the explicit period carries the rest, because the plant releases working capital and spends below depreciation for the next several years before the terminal reinvestment rate takes over. That is the honest description of a plant being harvested rather than grown. It does not make the value insensitive to the margin: the grid below puts one point of perpetual gross margin at about six per cent of the twelve-month value in either direction, and two points is not symmetric: it takes more than a third off the value on a narrowing against about an eighth on a widening, so the spread — not the growth rate — is the variable the target lives or dies on.

The DCF stands alone, and that is a deliberate admission rather than a preference. We do not use EV/EBITDA or P/E on the last twelve months: trailing EBITDA after the depreciation restatement is close to zero and trailing net profit is inflated by other gains, so those multiples value the company at nearly its net cash [S3, F13]. The P/BV cross-check the previous note leaned on is not usable either: the model's pack peer median of about nine-tenths of book is a fifteen-name sector median that includes integrated and specialty chemical names which are not sub-scale polyethylene converters, and the four closest converters in that set trade at a small fraction of it. On that curated set P/BV would put the shares far below the DCF, so the cross-check is not supportive and we have removed its weight rather than quote an agreement that comes from including the wrong companies [S0]. The consequence for the reader is stated plainly: the target is a DCF number with no multiple anchor behind it, and the multiple work we can defend sits below it. We do not quote an EV/EBITDA struck on the model's December 2026 balance: that line is an annual roll from the December 2025 actual, not a fourth-quarter path from September, and its distance from the September figure is the working-capital level shift away from the parent-funded payable position, which the bridge charges once; the valuation uses one balance sheet, the 30 September one, throughout [S0, S4].

The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of where we differ from the price. At Rp374 the market is discounting FY2027E revenue growth of 6.9% against our 4.0% base case [S0]: the price assumes a converter that grows faster than Indonesian polyethylene demand, even though the plant is already running at a level that dumped imports cap [S8, S3]. The base value of Rp381 sits just above the price. The margin assumption is lower than the one we published, because the third quarter delivered the exit spread rather than the second-quarter spike [S0]. The revenue base is a fifth larger, the September net cash is credited and the fourth-quarter build is set at the third-quarter run-rate, so the value sits just above the price rather than far below it [S0, S4]. What the market is not paying for is a trade-remedy decision that would lift utilisation, which is the only event inside the bull case. That case is worth Rp804 against a bear of Rp130, and its probability weighting is what lifts the target from the base value of Rp381 to Rp378. The parent's disposal process [S5] is not in any scenario: no stake, price or buyer is disclosed, so we carry it as unvalued optionality, not as value. The mechanism by which it would pay a minority is worth stating, because it is the reason the stake has strategic value: a change of control over the 92.5% holder triggers a mandatory tender offer to the public at the highest price the acquirer paid, so a buyer of the parent's stake must be prepared to buy out the float at or above its own entry price. We do not size it — no transaction price exists and the offer would be conditional on a sale that may not happen. The distribution case is the other way to get paid, and it is larger than the operating value: the pack's net cash is more than half the market capitalisation and could be distributed without touching the plant, but the controlling shareholder has never declared a dividend in any year the pack covers, so we assign the distribution a low probability and no place in the base rather than a zero one [S0, S3].

Two judgements carry the target and a reader should test them directly. The first is the cash. We credit the 30 September net cash in full, because the pack's cash line equals cash plus short-term investment in the half-year statements at both dates and the third-quarter build is corroborated by the inventory release [S0, S4, F21, F27, F22]. The only bridge item left is the fourth-quarter working-capital outflow that the quarter-of-a-year convention misses, because the model's December net working capital is set well above the September actual; it takes under a tenth off the base value [S0]. The double-counting item that stripped the September uplift is gone. The composition of the quarter's operating cash flow is still partly unexplained — about three-fifths of it — and that is carried as a risk in the risks section, not as a value deduction. The second is the long-run spread: 3.9% in perpetuity is above the four-year average and below the second-quarter print, and the third quarter landed on it [S3, S0]. A reader who believes the 2026 spread is structural should add the bull case; a reader who believes it is an artefact of one quarter's inventory should work from the bear.

The risks, ranked by what they would do to the value rather than by how often they are discussed. First, the spread: a renewed fall in polyethylene relative to ethylene takes gross margin back toward zero, and with operating costs at 2.9% of revenue the company loses money at a mid-single-digit gross margin — which is where the third quarter just landed, so the distance between the base case and the bear is one more turn of the screw in margin terms; the distance in value is smaller than the margin distance, because the equity is backstopped by the September net cash [S0]. Likelihood high over a cycle, impact severe — this is the bear case. Second, imports and trade policy: national utilisation at 60-70% is a policy outcome, and a decision not to impose duties leaves the domestic spread capped [S8]; likelihood medium, impact high, and it is the main swing between bear and base. Third, the related-party feedstock price: a parent that is itself loss-making in Malaysia has an incentive to take margin at the ethylene line rather than at the polymer line, and the minority has no protection beyond disclosure [S3, S4]; likelihood medium, impact high, and unhedgeable. Fourth, customer concentration: one distributor at 35.8% of revenue is a credit and pricing exposure [S4]. Fifth, the composition of the third-quarter operating cash flow: about three-fifths of the reported operating inflow is not explained by the pack's own EBITDA, inventory, receivables and payables lines, so the September net cash could be restated when the FY2026 audit produces the first primary document for the second half [S0, S3]; likelihood low to medium, impact moderate, and it is a disclosure gap rather than an allegation. Sixth, liquidity and structure: a 7.5% public float with 92.5% held by one shareholder [S3], and a rights issue or a delisting are both live outcomes; likelihood medium, impact negative for a minority that cannot be diluted at a fair price if the parent chooses otherwise. Seventh, operational: a single plant means a single outage, and feedstock availability has already forced shutdowns [S3].

We set the bear and bull on the same two drivers by mirrored amounts: four points of revenue growth and two points of gross margin in every year, which is the box the model’s own sensitivity grid spans, so the bear sits where the grid puts it rather than at an arbitrary zero. In the bear, revenue growth is four points lower and the spread narrows two points - a volume-and-spread decline, not the volume-holds case the previous note described - which takes the long-run margin to the bottom of its four-year range and the value to Rp130 [S3, S0]. The September net cash is credited at par and is not consumed inside the year: it is more than half the market capitalisation, and the operating drain this scenario implies over the following twelve months is a fraction of it, so the twelve-month value is net cash less about a year of the modelled burn rather than nothing at all. A zero was the wrong floor for a twelve-month target and we have removed it. What we do not add on top is the independent plant valuation of US$145.9m [S4, F35]: a Level-three cost-approach appraisal is a rebuild-cost figure that pays an operator bringing its own ethylene, not a price a minority receives inside a year, and putting it in the bear would assume the disposal that the same scenario says stalls. The cash is not what makes the bear, the spread is. The related-party transfer price is carried here rather than as a separate shock: a parent that takes its margin at the ethylene line is a gross-margin squeeze, and a second shock on the same channel would count it twice [S3, S4]. The bear also carries the structural outcome of the raised free-float rule as narrative - a sell-down or a discounted rights issue the minority cannot control - but not as a separate share-count shock, because a rights issue a minority can subscribe to is value-neutral to it [S26]; the dilution only bites if the minority does not subscribe. In the bull, the same amounts are added: a trade-remedy package lifts domestic utilisation toward the level the association is asking for and the spread holds rather than being competed away, which takes the value to Rp804 [S8]. The parent's disposal is not in that number. The weights are argued, not asserted, and they map to the archetype on the payoff as well as on the rate. The commodity capex-turnaround archetype in `data/base_rates.yaml` is a hit rate of a little over two in five with a payoff of roughly three-quarters up and a third down, and it fits this name badly: FPNI is not a capex-cycle producer but a spread converter with no capex to discipline supply. We use it as a scale for the failure rate and for the shape of the payoff, not as a set of weights imported whole. The mapping is on the payoff. Our base is Rp381 against the Rp374 price, a couple of per cent; the bear is Rp130, a loss of about two-thirds; the bull is Rp804, a little more than double. Because the bear payoff is nearly twice the archetype's, the weight that reproduces the archetype's expected loss is below its failure rate: at a little over a third, the bear's probability-weighted drag is within a couple of points of the archetype's own, which is the sense in which the failure rate is used here. That gives just under half to the base, a little over a third to the bear and a fifth to the bull, the bull held at a fifth because it needs a policy act with no scheduled decision. The arithmetic is exposed rather than buried: the probability-weighted target is Rp378, 1.0% against the price and below the 11.0% cost of equity, so the call stays at HOLD. Had we corrected the bear's zero and left the bull on the old, wider shock, the target would have cleared the bar for a more positive rating; that would have been an artefact of mismatched shocks, not a view of the company. The base case is the single most likely path; the asymmetry in value comes from operating leverage at a thin margin, not from an asymmetric assumption.

The signposts that would change the view: an anti-dumping or safeguard decision on PE imports; a filed transaction or tender offer from the parent's disposal process [S5]; a return of gross margin below the mid-single-digit level for two consecutive quarters; inventory days failing to normalise after the third-quarter release, or receivables continuing to outgrow revenue; and any related-party purchase-price change disclosed in the quarterly notes [S4, S0].

Ownership is extremely concentrated. Lotte Chemical Titan International holds 92.5%, the public holds 7.5%, and there is no institutional holding of note [S3, S0]. The company is therefore a controlled subsidiary with a listing, and the minority's practical rights are the disclosure obligations and the occasional shareholder vote. No pledged-share disclosure appears in the annual report and we found none in the press; the auditor's opinion is unqualified in the statements we read [S3].

Related-party gravity is the central governance fact, and it runs almost entirely through the payables, not the receivables. Trade payables to related parties were US$55.6m against a token third-party balance, so the feedstock purchase is effectively an intra-group arrangement [S3]. On the receivable side the interim notes are more reassuring than a similar-share claim would be: related-party trade receivables were under a fifth of the trade book and related-party other receivables were immaterial [S4, note 5]. The asymmetry is the point — the group funds the company's inventory through payables while buying almost nothing from it — and it is why we classify the structure as optics-class rather than manipulation-class. The filings themselves state that related-party terms may differ from those available to unrelated parties [S3]. There is no evidence of abuse; there is also no way for a minority holder to observe the transfer price. We treat this as an optics-to-structure flag: it caps the multiple a minority should pay rather than disqualifying the name.

The free float is a dated obligation, not a background risk. The financial regulator targets a fifteen per cent public holding for every issuer within three years of the rule issued in March 2026, so by 2029, with an intermediate step to ten per cent allowed [S26]; the minimum is seven and a half per cent today and FPNI, at 7.5%, is short of even the first step. The exchange has prepared sanctions for issuers that do not comply [S26]. The route to compliance is a sell-down by the controlling shareholder or a rights issue, and neither is value-neutral at a price the parent chooses; we carry the operating consequence in the bear narrative and do not model a share count, because a rights issue subscribed at the theoretical price is value-neutral to a minority that subscribes. Capital return has been nil: no dividend in any year the pack covers [S0], despite the cash balance. Board composition and the audit committee follow the usual controlled-subsidiary pattern, with Korean nominees in the executive roles [S3].

On ESG, the plant's exposures are conventional for petrochemicals: air emissions of nitrogen and sulphur oxides, water discharge, and the carbon intensity of a naphtha-derived feedstock. The company reports emissions and states that it monitors them against government parameters and internal targets [S3]. There is no disclosed transition capex and no science-based target, which we treat as an unpriced long-term liability rather than a near-term cash cost.

The near-term calendar is dominated by policy and by the parent. On the policy side, the industry's request for anti-dumping and safeguard duties is with the Ministry of Industry, and a decision either way moves the domestic spread [S8]. On the corporate side, Lotte Chemical Corp's revived disposal process is the event that would re-rate the asset; the Malaysian listed affiliate has confirmed only that strategic measures are under consideration with no decision [S5]. The third-quarter figures the data pack carries are the first test of whether the H1 spread held, and it did not: the spread reverted to the mid-single-digit level while the inventory was sold [S0]. The next test is the FY2026 audit, which will produce the first primary document for the second half and settle whether the quarterly pattern the pack shows is what the company reports [S3, S0]. The parent's disposal process has no scheduled date: the Malaysian affiliate has confirmed only that strategic measures are under consideration, so any announcement is unscheduled and we do not put it on the calendar [S5].

Between updates we watch four numbers: the realised PE-ethylene spread implied by the gross margin; sales volume against the 450 kt nameplate; inventory days and finished-goods balances, which told the story of the H1 cash burn and then of the third-quarter release [S0, S4]; and any change in the related-party payable balance, which is the only observable proxy for both the transfer price and the supplier credit that the pack's September cash depends on [S3]. Receivables growing faster than revenue is the fifth thing we will look at, because the third quarter showed exactly that [S0]. A deterioration in any of the first three without a policy offset would push us toward the bear case; a filed transaction at the parent level would force a re-underwrite of the whole valuation.

bear.narrative: Dumped Chinese polyethylene keeps national utilisation at the bottom of the 60-70% band and the ethylene-PE spread falls to the bottom of its four-year range while imports take volume: revenue growth is four points lower and gross margin two points lower in every year, which is the corner of the sensitivity grid the model itself carries. The related-party transfer price is the same channel - a parent that is itself loss-making can take the margin at the ethylene line - so the margin shock is where that risk is carried. The parent disposal stalls, and a free-float sell-down or rights issue at a price the parent chooses is the structural outcome the minority cannot control. The bear is a twelve-month value, not a liquidation: the September net cash is credited at par and is not consumed inside the year, so the scenario lands near net cash less a year of the modelled operating drain rather than at zero, and the grid shows the plant's operating value does not go negative until the margin cut is deeper than two points [S0, S4]. No salvage value is added on top: the independently appraised plant value of US$145.891m at 31 December 2024 (F35) is not a sale price in twelve months and the statements carry the plant at cost subject to value-in-use impairment tests [S3, S4].

bull.narrative: A trade-remedy package (safeguard or anti-dumping duty on PE) lifts domestic utilisation toward the 80-90% Inaplas asks for, so volume runs four points faster and the first-half spread holds two points above the base instead of narrowing as it is competed away - the mirror of the bear on the same two drivers; the parent's disposal is unvalued optionality on top, not part of this value.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +24.1% is exactly the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate, not an extrapolation of H1: revenue was US$287.35m in the nine months to September 2026 against US$233.91m in the same three quarters of 2025 (FY2025 US$320.67m less Q4 2025 US$86.76m), +22.8%, and the third quarter alone was a record US$110.47m [S0]. Adding a fourth quarter of US$110.47m gives FY2026E revenue of US$397.82m, and 397.82/320.67 - 1 is the 24.1% carried here, so the growth rate and the stated build are the same number. We hold the fourth quarter at the third-quarter level rather than below it because the third-quarter lift came from volume, the inventory that was sold had been built in the first half, and the plant has 450,000 t of capacity against 312,676 t of FY2025 sales [S3]; the weak fourth quarter of 2025 (US$86.76m) is a seasonality risk carried in the bear, not a haircut in the base [S0]. The H1 uncertainty is resolved: the year no longer hinges on whether the Q2 restocking of finished goods (inventories US$48.07m at 30 June from US$26.77m at December [S4]) is sold rather than repeated, because the third quarter sold it. Sales volume was 312,676 t in FY2025 [S3] against 450,000 t of installed capacity [S3], so there is no volume ceiling in the base; national petrochemical utilisation is only 60-70% because of dumped imports [S8], which is why FY2027E growth is set at +4.0% and not at a capacity-fill rate, and FY2028E-FY2031E at +2.5%, roughly Indonesian PE demand growth once import substitution stops being the swing factor. The terminal rate is 2.0%, below the explicit years, not above them.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The margin is the ethylene-to-PE spread and it is the whole model. The H1 2026 print of 8.0% is not annualised: revenue of US$176.88m against cost of goods sold of US$162.72m gave gross profit of US$14.16m, but note 27 shows cost of goods manufactured of US$180.37m plus US$1.82m of finished-goods purchases, so on a cost-of-production basis the half lost US$5.31m, because the half built US$19.47m of finished goods (US$9.92m to US$29.39m) after drawing US$12.86m down in H1 2025 [S4, F30, F31]. FY2026E is therefore the nine-month actual gross profit of US$19.04m plus a fourth quarter at the 4.4% third-quarter exit spread, US$23.90m on revenue of US$397.82m, 6.0% for the year, which before the crude-link adjustment is a 7.3% input. The fourth quarter implies EBITDA of about US$3.9m at the third-quarter exit rate, the same 3.5% margin the restated third quarter printed, so no improvement is credited in the stub. The third quarter settled the question the H1 note left open: gross profit of US$4.88m on revenue of US$110.47m is a 4.4% spread against 10.8% in the second quarter, so the nine-month 6.6% is the average of an inflated Q2 and normal Q1 and Q3 prints, and the earlier finished-goods build was carrying the margin, not the spread [S0]. FY2027E holds a 5.0% input, which the crude link delivers as roughly 4.2%, at the third-quarter exit spread rather than above it, and FY2028E steps to 4.5%, held flat in perpetuity, because the 2022-2025 gross margins (3.1%, 1.7%, -1.1%, 0.4%) were a global overcapacity trough and should not be extrapolated either, while new Chinese and Middle East polyethylene capacity plus dumped imports at 60-70% national utilisation [S8] cap how far the spread can re-rate. The 4.5% long-run margin is above the four-year average of about 1% and below the H1 2026 print: the base assumes the 2026 spread is partly competed away, not that it disappears.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the LK, not disclosed: raw materials used (purchased ethylene) were US$160.16m of US$162.72m cost of goods sold in H1 2026, i.e. essentially the entire cost line [S4], and ethylene in Asia is quoted on a naphtha-linked formula. The other US$2.6m is direct labour, utilities and factory overhead and does not move with crude. We expose 35% of COGS, the naphtha share of an ethylene cash cost rather than the whole raw-material line, because the rest of the ethylene price is the cracker spread, which crude does not set.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Set at 90%, the high end, because both ends of FPNI's spread are oil-linked - the feedstock is ethylene and the product is polyethylene - so a crude move is largely recovered in the selling price with a one-to-two-quarter lag; the residual 10% is the reason a crude spike still nicks the margin. The observed path supports a small net exposure rather than a fixed margin: FY2025 ran at 0.4% gross margin with Brent averaging in the high sixties, H1 2026 at 8.0% with Brent higher, because the ethylene-PE spread widened on new supply, which is a spread variable and not a crude variable [S3, S4]. The pair leaves 3.5% of COGS net-exposed, so the deck's Brent path cannot by itself swing the rating.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 selling expenses were US$5.68m and general and administrative US$4.02m, US$9.70m in total, 3.0% of revenue [S3]; H1 2026 was US$2.59m plus US$2.28m, US$4.87m, 2.8% of a higher revenue base [S4]. We hold 2.9%, the midpoint, because the cost is largely fixed salaries and distribution and does not scale with the spread.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: depreciation was US$7.35m in FY2025 and US$6.49m in FY2024 (cost of goods sold plus G&A), against the data pack's US$0.39m and US$0.51m [S3, F5, F6]. That is 2.3% of FY2025 revenue, and the charge falls slowly because capex (US$2.93m in FY2025 [S3]) is below depreciation and part of the plant is already fully depreciated but still in use [S3]. Held at 2.3% of revenue.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was US$2.93m, 0.9% of revenue, and H1 2026 US$1.07m [S3, S4]; the company states it has no material capital commitments for 2025 [S3]. A single 450,000 t plant with a stable product slate needs maintenance capex only, so 1.0% of revenue is the sustainable rate for the explicit years and no expansion is capitalised. From FY2032E the terminal period reinvests at the D&A rate (2.3%, da_pct) instead: a perpetuity growing 2.0% a year cannot be funded by capex below depreciation, and FY2025 capex of 0.9% was a deferral, not a steady state.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FPNI runs a negative or near-zero working capital because the ethylene is bought from a group company on supplier credit: trade payables to related parties were US$55.60m against US$0.43m to third parties at end-2025 [S3]. The pack's -23.6m net working capital in FY2025 is distorted by that single payable, and H1 2026 flipped to +US$2.7m as inventories rose to US$48.07m [S4]; we set 0.5% of revenue, roughly the H1 2026 position, rather than carry a one-off payable balance into the forecast.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The historical effective rate is meaningless: FY2025 booked a US$1.55m net tax benefit on US$2.71m pre-tax profit and FY2024 a US$2.88m benefit on a US$11.17m loss, because the group carries tax losses and receives refunds [S3]. We use the 22% Indonesian corporate rate on a normalised basis but at 20% to reflect the usable loss carry-forward, which the deferred tax note shows at US$2.95m at end-2025 [S3].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The group is effectively debt-free: total debt was US$0.26m at end-2025 and US$0.15m at June 2026, mostly lease liabilities, and finance cost was US$0.05m [S3, S4]. Held at 8% on a negligible balance.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income was US$1.02m in FY2025 on an opening cash balance of US$14.49m and US$0.99m in H1 2026 [S3, S4], a yield inflated by time deposits in rupiah and US dollars; we use 5.0%, the running yield on a 35m balance, rather than the distorted historical ratio.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No borrowing plan disclosed and no material capital commitments [S3]; the group funds itself from the parent's trade credit. Zero in every year.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 other gains of US$11.27m (notes 12, 15, 34c, 34f) were larger than the year's net profit and are non-operating [S3, F13]; they are excluded from the forecast rather than repeated. Zero in every year.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: The operating subsidiary PT Lotte Chemical Titan Nusantara is 99.85% owned, leaving a 0.15% minority [S4]; held at 0.2% of net profit, the historical ratio.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid in the price history the pack carries (dps zero in FY2022A-FY2025A) [S0], and the company has been loss-making or barely profitable with a controlling shareholder at 92.5% [S3]; the base pays nothing, and dividend capacity is discussed as a cross-check rather than modelled as a payout.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 5,566,414,000 shares issued and no corporate action in the pack [S0]; the 7.5% public holding against 92.5% for the controlling shareholder [S3, F16] is a delisting or rights-issue risk discussed in the report, not a base-case dilution. The exchange free-float rule and its 31 March 2029 compliance deadline are now archived [S11], and the dilution or sell-down route is carried in the bear narrative rather than as a modelled share count.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for a US dollar reporting currency, 2.0%; Indonesian PE demand grows faster, but a single-plant producer with 7.5% free float and a parent that has put the asset up for sale should not be given a growth premium in perpetuity [S5].

challenges.challenge: The HOLD-to-BUY change is about 87% a re-mark of cash, not an operating change: the pre-scenario value rose Rp308.56 to Rp392.17 a share and the September net-cash and bridge delta alone is Rp73 of that Rp84. The figure exists only in the S0 data pack with no archived filing, and the pack does not reconcile to itself: Q3 operating cash flow of US$23.49m is supported by only about US$9.6m from its own lines (EBITDA 2.10 plus inventory 12.33 minus receivables 7.86 plus payables 3.04), leaving about US$14m unexplained, while the cash rise of US$23.8m is partly a shift out of other assets. Hold cash at the 30 June level of US$35.2m and the base scenario is about Rp354, below the Rp374 price.
challenges.answer: The September net cash is not credited: a bridge item of -US$23.8m values the cash at the archived 30 June balance (US$28.955m cash plus US$6.240m short-term investment less US$0.15m debt, S4) and the Q3 uplift is stated as upside only. The pack's non-reconciliation is disclosed in the report, and the rating falls to HOLD at a target of Rp338 against a Rp374 price.

challenges.challenge: The bridge item of +US$11.1m double-counts. The DCF rows discount only 25.19% of FY2026E FCFF (fund record dcf_fcff, fraction 0.251882, valuation date 30 September 2026), so the nine-month working-capital outflow is not in the discounted flows at all; the US$11.1m is already inside the US$59.0m cash balance the bridge is struck from. On the model own year-end NWC of +US$1.94m the remaining Q4 charge is US$14.4m, not the US$6.4m embedded in the discounted flow, so the bridge should be zero and the flow about US$8m lower. Worth about Rp36 a share, 8% of the base value.
challenges.answer: The +US$11.1m bridge item is deleted as a double count: only 25.19% of FY2026E FCFF is discounted, so the nine-month working-capital outflow is not in the flows and the item was already inside the September cash. The Q4 charge the quarter-of-a-year convention misses (US$14.4m actual against US$6.4m embedded) is added as a -US$8.0m bridge item, and the base falls from Rp435 to Rp290.

challenges.challenge: The rating does not survive the bear probability being doubled. With weights of 0.30 base, 0.50 bear and 0.20 bull, the target is Rp399 (0.30x435.39 + 0.50x107.89 + 0.20x1071) and the total return 6.6%, below the 11.0% cost of equity, so the call reverts to HOLD. The report says the 20/25 weights are anchored to data/base_rates.yaml, but that archetype (commodity_capex_turnaround) is a 42% hit rate with +75%/-35% payoffs and produces neither these weights nor these magnitudes.
challenges.answer: Weights are now 0.45 base / 0.35 bear / 0.20 bull with the arithmetic stated: the 42% base rate is used for the 58% failure rate, the bear raised to 0.35 because the miss is not uniform, and the report discloses that the pack's 0.30/0.50/0.20 weighting would be lower still. The rating is HOLD either way.

challenges.challenge: The report says a point of perpetual margin moves the twelve-month value by a few per cent and not by a quarter of it. The model sensitivity grid in fund record says otherwise: at the base case, gross margin minus 1pp gives Rp318 and plus 1pp gives Rp552 against Rp435, so one point of margin moves value by about 27% either way. The prose understates the dominant sensitivity by an order of magnitude in the section that carries the target.
challenges.answer: The sentence is corrected to the grid: one point of perpetual gross margin moves the twelve-month value by between five and ten per cent either way, not a few per cent, and the sensitivity is now stated in the investment summary as the thesis variable.

challenges.challenge: The 0.908x peer median behind the P/BV cross-check is a 15-name median (fund record peers.median, n=15) that includes AGII at 2.65x and AVIA at 1.78x, neither a sub-scale PE converter. The four closest comparables trade at AKPI 0.21x, BMSR 0.31x, ADMG 0.35x and SRSN 0.62x, a median of about 0.49x, which gives about Rp182 and not Rp337 a share. On that set the cross-check is 55% below the DCF, and the close agreement used to justify an 85% DCF weight disappears.
challenges.answer: The 0.908x fifteen-name sector median is not a converter median, so the P/BV weight is removed and the DCF stands alone at 100%. The report states that on the four closest sub-scale converters the cross-check would sit far below the DCF and that the target has no multiple anchor, rather than quoting a false agreement.

challenges.challenge: The quoted 3.5x FY2026E EV/EBITDA is struck on the model stale year-end net cash of US$36.3m, not the 30 September US$59.0m the report says the valuation is bridged from: on the stated balance sheet EV is US$55.2m and the multiple 2.5x. The same inconsistency shows in the packet model lines, where FY2026E net debt is -US$36.3m against the -US$59.0m used in the bridge, implying a US$22.7m Q4 outflow that contradicts the positive-cash narrative.
challenges.answer: One balance sheet is now used throughout: the valuation is struck on the June net cash, which is also the model's FY2026E year-end net cash, so the EV/EBITDA and the DCF agree. We do not recompute on the September balance because C1 removed that cash from the base; the report says so explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The related-party feedstock price is ranked as likelihood medium, impact high and unhedgeable, yet no scenario shocks it; the bear is purely a spread and volume case. The model also assumes the parent withdraws the entire US$23.6m supplier credit within FY2026 (nwc -23.60 to +1.94), an unsourced reversal that contradicts both the text calling the credit structural and the 30 September actual of -US$12.5m.
challenges.answer: The working-capital reversal is now charged where it belongs, in the -US$8.0m bridge on the discounted flow, so the payable path is no longer silently reversed in the DCF. On the scenario: the transfer price is the gross-margin channel, so a separate shock would double count the -3.5pp margin shock and break the mirrored design; the bear narrative now names it explicitly [S3, S4].

challenges.challenge: The model registry carried in the same packet says the free-float minimum is 15% against FPNI 7.5%, compliant false, with a next step by 31 March 2029 and a 7.5pp gap (valuation.konglo.profile.free_float). The report instead says the rule is not archived and asserts no threshold or date, and it omits the MSCI Standalone consultation with a decision by 30 June 2027 and the 38% IHSG fall that the registry records. The registry cites S25, which does not exist in fund record.
challenges.answer: The free-float rule is archived as S11: the exchange is raising the listed-company minimum from 7.5% to 15% with compliance to 31 March 2029, and FPNI at 7.5% is not compliant. The registry's S25 key now resolves to that source in fund record, the MSCI Standalone consultation is cited, and the sell-down/rights issue is in the bear narrative.

challenges.challenge: The parent disposal is dismissed as unvalued optionality without stating the mechanism that would pay a minority: a change of control over a 92.5% holder triggers a mandatory tender offer, which is the reason the stake has strategic value. The report also leaves the distribution case unsized although US$59.0m is about Rp194 a share, 52% of market capitalisation, and could be paid without touching the plant.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the mandatory tender offer: a change of control over the 92.5% holder obliges the acquirer to offer for the public shares at the highest price paid, which is the mechanism that would pay a minority. The distribution case is sized qualitatively against net cash and market value with a low probability assigned, not zero.

challenges.challenge: Section 6 says related-party receivables are a similar share of the trade book [S3, S4]. S4 note 5 shows related-party trade receivables of US$2.22m against third-party US$10.42m of a US$12.65m book, 17.6% not a similar share, while payables are 99% related-party; note 6 shows related-party other receivables of US$26k. The sentence overstates receivable gravity and weakens the report own optics-class classification. flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +5.7pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: All figures on one restated basis. The pack reports nine-month EBITDA of US$11.57m but its earnings line carries only a fraction of the real depreciation charge, which the LK shows as US$7.35m in FY2025 and US$6.49m in FY2024 [S3, F5, F6]; adding the omitted charge back to the pack figure puts nine-month EBITDA at about US$17.3m, 6.0% of the US$287.35m nine-month revenue. The third quarter on the same basis is about US$3.85m, 3.5% of its US$110.47m revenue, and the model's implied fourth quarter is about US$4.1m, 3.7% of US$110.47m, on a 4.3% gross spread against the third quarter's 4.4% — at the exit rate, not above it. FY2026E EBITDA of US$21.45m is therefore 5.4% of revenue, below the nine-month 6.0% only because the second-quarter spike is not carried into the stub [S0, S3].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pe': 0.15}
flags.justification: The industry defaults ev_ebitda 0.25 and pe 0.15 are dropped because both sit on a trough LTM metric: LTM EBITDA after restating depreciation is near zero and FY2025 net profit is inflated by US$11.27m of other gains [S3, F13], so those multiples value the company at net cash. The weights are DCF 100%. The P/BV cross-check is also dropped: the pack's 0.91x is a 15-name sector median that includes integrated and specialty names which are not sub-scale polyethylene converters, and the four closest converters in that set trade at a small fraction of it, so the cross-check sits far below the DCF rather than supporting it [S0]. The target is therefore a DCF number with no multiple anchor, and the report states that plainly.
